keywords: how much grass seed do I need
takeaways: Seed needed = area in sq ft / 1,000 x the rate in lb per 1,000 sq ft for your grass type.
Tall fescue needs 6 to 8 lb per 1,000 sq ft for a new lawn, and Kentucky bluegrass needs only 2 to 3 lb.
Overseeding rates are about half the new lawn rate for most cool-season grasses.
body:
A new tall fescue lawn needs 6 to 8 lb of seed per 1,000 sq ft, so a 5,000 sq ft yard needs 30 to 40 lb. Kentucky bluegrass needs far less, 2 to 3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, because the seed is much smaller. This guide gives the rates by grass type, the formula, and a worked example you can check before you buy.

## The formula and the rates

**Seed needed in lb = (area in sq ft / 1,000) x rate in lb per 1,000 sq ft.**

Measure each lawn section, add the areas, and leave out driveways, beds, and patios. Our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) helps with odd shapes and circles around trees.

Rates below come from university extension guides. Kansas State, Nebraska, and Penn State publish the same core rates for the main cool-season grasses.

| Grass type | New lawn, lb per 1,000 sq ft | Overseeding, lb per 1,000 sq ft |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tall fescue | 6 to 8 | 3 to 4 |
| Kentucky bluegrass | 2 to 3 | 1 to 1.5 |
| Perennial ryegrass | 4 to 5 | 4 to 6 for renovation overseeding |
| Fine fescues | 4 to 5 | 2 to 2.5 |
| Bluegrass and ryegrass mix | 2 to 3 | 1 to 1.5 |

Penn State lists tall fescue at 6 to 8 lb, Kentucky bluegrass at 2 to 3 lb, perennial ryegrass at 4 to 5 lb, and fine fescues at 4 to 5 lb per 1,000 sq ft for new lawns. Kansas State gives the same tall fescue and bluegrass rates and says to use about half the new lawn rate for overseeding or shade. Nebraska gives the same full rates and the same half rate rule for seeding into an existing lawn.

Warm-season grasses run lower. Extension and seed guides list Bermudagrass at about 1 to 2 lb per 1,000 sq ft. If your bag label gives a rate, use the label rate for that exact blend. A mix follows the rate of its main grass by weight.

## Worked example: a 5,000 sq ft new tall fescue lawn

Your back yard measures 50 x 100 ft (15.2 x 30.5 m). The soil is bare and raked. You choose turf-type tall fescue and a middle rate of 7 lb per 1,000 sq ft.

Step 1: Area = 50 x 100 = 5,000 sq ft.

Step 2: Units of 1,000 sq ft = 5,000 / 1,000 = 5.

Step 3: Seed = 5 x 7 lb = 35 lb.

Step 4: Round up like a buyer. Seed is sold in set bag sizes, so buy 40 lb, for example two 20 lb bags or one larger bag plus a small bag for patch work. That gives you a little extra for thin spots at the edges.

Check the math a second way. At 7 lb per 1,000 sq ft, each pound covers 1,000 / 7 = about 143 sq ft. For 5,000 sq ft, 5,000 / 143 = 34.97 lb, which rounds to the same 35 lb before bag rounding. Both methods agree.

If the same yard were an overseed job, use half the rate. 5 x 3.5 lb = 17.5 lb, rounded up to a 20 lb bag. Overseeding a thin lawn with a full new lawn rate wastes seed and packs seedlings too tight.

## How to measure and split the yard

Break the yard into rectangles. Front, back, and each side strip get their own length x width. Add them, then subtract large beds and hardscape. A 10 x 20 ft bed is 200 sq ft, about 1.4 lb of tall fescue seed at a 7 lb rate.

For a circle, use radius x radius x 3.14. A ring with a 10 ft radius is about 314 sq ft. For slopes, measure along the ground, not on a flat map view.

Seed in two passes. Put half the seed in the spreader and walk one direction. Put in the other half and walk at a right angle. Nebraska extension recommends this method, and it hides spreader misses that show up as stripes later.

## What changes the rate you should use

Shade lowers the effective rate for some grasses and raises failure risk for others. Fine fescues handle shade best among cool-season grasses, which is why Penn State lists them for full shade at 4 to 5 lb. Tall fescue in shade can go at the half rate Kansas State notes when you overseed, but a new shady lawn still needs good soil contact to take hold.

Seed size explains the big rate gaps. A pound of Kentucky bluegrass holds far more seeds than a pound of tall fescue. More seed by weight does not mean more plants. Follow the rate for the species, not a general pounds-per-yard guess.

Soil contact changes how much of your seed lives. Seed on top of thatch or thick clippings dries out and fails. Mow low, rake or aerate, and get seed down to soil. If you plan to cover bare patches with mulch after other bed work, keep seed and mulch jobs separate and use our [mulch calculator](/blog/mulch-calculator/) for the beds.

Timing matters too. Early fall is the best window for cool-season seed in most of the US. Spring seeding works, but weeds compete hard. If you need fast cover, compare seed with sod using our [sod calculator](/blog/sod-calculator/) notes in the new topics list.

## Mistakes that waste seed

The first mistake is seeding too heavy. Extension guides warn that too much seed raises disease risk and stress damage, and crowded seedlings stay weak. More is not safer. Hit the rate and stop.

The second mistake is seeding too light to save money. A thin rate leaves gaps, weeds fill them, and you buy seed twice. The gap between 30 lb and 35 lb on a 5,000 sq ft lawn is one small bag. Buy the full rate.

The third mistake is one pass in one direction. Missed lines stay bare for weeks. Two half-rate passes at right angles fix most spreader error.

The fourth mistake is letting seed dry out. Keep the top half inch of soil moist with light watering two to four times a day for the first two weeks, as Nebraska extension advises. Deep, rare watering is for an established lawn, not for germination.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much grass seed do I need per 1,000 sq ft?
It depends on the grass. New lawn rates are 6 to 8 lb for tall fescue, 2 to 3 lb for Kentucky bluegrass, 4 to 5 lb for perennial ryegrass, and 4 to 5 lb for fine fescues, per extension guides. Check your bag label for a blend rate.

### How much seed for a 10,000 sq ft lawn?
At a middle tall fescue rate of 7 lb per 1,000 sq ft, 10,000 sq ft needs 70 lb. At a Kentucky bluegrass rate of 2.5 lb, the same area needs 25 lb. Round up to whole bags sold in your store.

### Is overseeding half the new lawn rate?
For most cool-season grasses, yes. Kansas State and Nebraska both give about half the new lawn rate for overseeding. Perennial ryegrass used for renovation overseeding is an exception in the Penn State table, at 4 to 6 lb per 1,000 sq ft.

### How long does grass seed take to come up?
Perennial ryegrass is fastest, often 5 to 10 days. Tall fescue is often 7 to 14 days. Kentucky bluegrass is slow, often 14 to 28 days. Keep the seedbed moist the whole time or the count you planted will not be the count that grows.

### Can I put down too much grass seed?
Yes. Extension guides warn that over-seeding crowds seedlings, raises disease risk, and wastes money. Stick to the published rate for your grass type and save leftover seed, kept dry, for patch work.
